title: Capsule Wardrobe Packing: 5-4-3-2-1 Method and Examples
h1: How to pack a travel capsule wardrobe with the 5-4-3-2-1 method
excerpt: Capsule wardrobe packing made simple: how the 5-4-3-2-1 method works, carry-on lists for a warm, cold and work trip, and a short checklist to finish.
tldr: Pack five tops, four bottoms, three pairs of shoes, two layers or dresses and one accessory set, all in two neutrals plus one or two colours, so everything mixes. Wear your bulkiest pieces while travelling, plan one wash, and add underwear, socks and toiletries on top of the count.
body:
Capsule wardrobe packing means choosing a small set of clothes in a few colours that all work together, so a handful of pieces makes a week of outfits. The easiest way to start is the 5-4-3-2-1 method: five tops, four bottoms, three pairs of shoes, two dresses or layers and one accessory set, plus underwear, socks and sleepwear. If every top goes with every bottom, that's 20 combinations before you count the layers, and it fits in a carry-on for most week-long trips.

Below: how the method works (there are two versions), how to pick the pieces, three worked examples for a warm trip, a cold trip and a work trip, and a short checklist for everything that isn't clothing.

The 5-4-3-2-1 packing method

Nobody seems to agree who came up with it, and you'll find two versions online. The more common one counts shoes as the "3"; the other, used by AAA, counts accessories as the "3" and keeps shoes to two.

NumberCommon versionAAA's version
5TopsTops
4BottomsBottoms
3Pairs of shoesAccessories (belt, hat, watch)
2Dresses, swimwear or layering piecesPairs of shoes
1Accessory set (hat, scarf, sunglasses)One extra must-have, such as a jacket or swimsuit

Both versions leave out underwear, socks, sleepwear and toiletries, so add those separately. Shoes are the real difference. They're the heaviest, bulkiest thing in the bag, so if you can manage with two pairs (one worn for travel), the second version saves the most space.

The method works best for trips of about a week. For a long weekend it's more than you need; a smaller formula such as the 3-3-3 rule (three tops, three bottoms, three pairs of shoes) is closer to the mark. For longer trips, keep the same numbers and plan a wash rather than packing more.

Another pattern you'll see is the 1-2-3-4-5-6 rule: one hat, two pairs of shoes, three bottoms, four tops, five pairs of socks and six pairs of underwear. It's handy because it counts the small things the 5-4-3-2-1 method leaves out.

Capsule wardrobe packing in five steps

  1. List the days, not the outfits. Write down what each day involves: travel, walking, a beach, a meeting, a nice dinner. Most trips have three or four kinds of day, and you need clothes for each kind, not a new outfit for every day.
  2. Check the forecast and the evenings. Look at the range, not the average. A city that's 28°C at noon can drop to 15°C at night, and air-conditioned trains and offices are cold almost everywhere.
  3. Pick two neutrals and one or two colours. Navy and white, black and grey, olive and stone. Everything packed should work with both neutrals, so any top goes with any bottom.
  4. Choose fabrics that travel. Merino wool and many synthetic blends shrug off creases and can usually go a few wears between washes. Linen keeps you cool but creases quickly, which is fine if you like the relaxed look. Thick denim is heavy and slow to dry.
  5. Test it at home. Lay everything out and make an outfit for each kind of day. Anything that only works in one outfit stays at home, unless it's something like swimwear.

If you'd like help with the pairing step, a digital wardrobe app can suggest outfits from photos of your clothes. FitWardrobe is our app, and it isn't available yet; it suggests an outfit for an occasion you choose, from clothes you've photographed, but it doesn't make packing lists, and its suggestions need an internet connection.

Warm trip: a week in a carry-on

Say seven days somewhere around 25 to 32°C, with sightseeing, a beach day and a couple of dinners out. Palette: navy, white and stone, with one coloured top.

  • 5 tops: two plain cotton T-shirts (white and navy), one striped T-shirt, one linen shirt, one smarter top or knitted polo for evenings.
  • 4 bottoms: lightweight trousers (worn for travel), linen trousers, and two from shorts, a skirt or a second pair of shorts.
  • 3 pairs of shoes: comfortable trainers (worn for travel), sandals, and one smarter pair such as loafers or espadrilles.
  • 2 extras: a light overshirt or cardigan for planes and air conditioning, and swimwear.
  • 1 accessory set: sunglasses and a cap or sun hat.

The linen shirt doubles as a cover-up at the beach and a smart layer at dinner. Plan a sink wash or laundry stop around day four and you won't run short of T-shirts.

Cold trip: a week near freezing

Cold trips bend the formula. Bulky layers take the space that shoes and extra bottoms would use, so the numbers shift towards tops and layers. Say a week at 5°C to below freezing, mostly city walking.

  • Worn for travel: warm coat, boots, jeans or wool trousers, a jumper, and a thin base layer underneath. This is the heaviest outfit you own for the trip, and it doesn't take up bag space.
  • 5 tops: two merino or thermal base layers, two long-sleeved tops or shirts, and one more jumper.
  • 3 bottoms: dark trousers or a second pair of jeans, one smarter pair for evenings, and thermal leggings to wear underneath on the coldest days.
  • 2 pairs of shoes: the boots you wear, plus trainers or smarter shoes for indoors and evenings.
  • 2 layers: a packable down or fleece mid-layer, and the coat you're wearing.
  • 1 accessory set: a warm hat, gloves and a scarf.

Layering does the work here: base layer, top, jumper, mid-layer, coat. On a mild day you drop two of those. Wool socks are worth the space, and a pair of gloves you can use a phone in saves a lot of fumbling.

Work trip: business casual pieces and pairings

A three-day work trip is where a capsule pays off most, because you need to look put together every day with very little in the bag. These business casual pieces cover meetings, a dinner and the trip home. If you're not sure what the office or client expects, our guide to what to wear to work explains each dress code.

  • A navy unstructured jacket (worn for travel)
  • Two pairs of trousers: charcoal and stone
  • Four tops: white shirt, light blue shirt, fine merino knit, plain dark T-shirt
  • Two pairs of shoes: leather shoes or loafers (worn), clean plain trainers
  • One belt that works with both pairs of shoes
DayPairing
Day 1: travel and an afternoon meetingNavy jacket, white shirt, charcoal trousers, loafers
Day 2: full day of meetingsNavy jacket, light blue shirt, stone trousers, loafers
Day 2: team dinnerMerino knit, charcoal trousers, loafers
Day 3: morning meeting, flight homeNavy jacket, dark T-shirt, stone trousers, trainers

Every top works with both trousers and with or without the jacket, so if a shirt gets a coffee stain you still have options. If your office is more formal, swap the T-shirt for a third shirt and the trainers for a second pair of leather shoes.

Trips longer than a week

Don't pack more; wash more. The same 15 or so pieces will cover two weeks or two months if you do laundry every five or six days. Booking at least one stay with a washing machine makes this easy. Otherwise a sink wash works: a detergent sheet, a few minutes of scrubbing, then roll each piece in a towel to squeeze the water out and hang it overnight. Merino and synthetic tops are usually dry by morning. Jeans and thick cotton are not, which is one more reason to leave the second pair of jeans at home.

Packing it into the bag

Rolling suits T-shirts, knitwear and casual trousers. Folding flat is better for shirts and tailored pieces, and packing cubes stop everything shifting around. Stuff socks and chargers inside shoes, and put the shoes heel-to-toe along the edges of the case.

Wear the bulkiest outfit while travelling: boots, coat, jumper. Check your airline's cabin bag limits before you pack. They vary a lot between airlines and fare types, and some cheaper fares only include a small bag that fits under the seat.

A short checklist for everything else

  • Documents: passport or ID, visas if needed, bookings, insurance details, a copy of each somewhere other than your phone.
  • Money: a card that works abroad without high fees, and a little local cash.
  • Health: prescription medicines in their original packaging, painkillers, plasters, sunscreen.
  • Tech: phone charger, plug adaptor, power bank (usually carry-on only), headphones.
  • Toiletries: travel sizes, packed in a clear bag if your departure airport still limits liquids.
  • Underwear and socks: enough for the days until your first wash, plus one spare.
  • Laundry kit: a bag for dirty clothes and a few detergent sheets for a sink wash.

Before you zip the bag, check each item against your list of days. If you can't name the day you'll wear something, take it out. For more on building the everyday version of this wardrobe, see what a capsule wardrobe is and how to build one, or how to plan a week of outfits once you're home.

faq.a: It's a packing formula for about a week of travel: five tops, four bottoms, three pairs of shoes, two dresses, swimsuits or layers, and one accessory set such as a hat and sunglasses. Some versions swap the numbers so you pack three accessories and only two pairs of shoes. Underwear, socks, sleepwear and toiletries are packed on top of the count.

faq.q: How many outfits do I need for a 7-day trip?
faq.a: Fewer than seven complete, separate outfits. Five tops and four bottoms that all work together give up to 20 combinations, and most people repeat bottoms and shoes several times in a week without anyone noticing. Plan one outfit for each kind of day on the trip, such as travel, sightseeing and dinner, then fill the rest by mixing.

faq.q: What is the 3-3-3 rule for packing?
faq.a: The 3-3-3 rule means packing three tops, three bottoms and three pairs of shoes, nine pieces in total, plus underwear and toiletries. Three tops and three bottoms make nine top-and-bottom pairings. It suits a long weekend or a short work trip better than a full week, unless you're happy to do laundry halfway through.

faq.q: Can you fit a week of clothes in a carry-on?
faq.a: Yes, for most warm or mild trips, if you stick to a capsule of around 15 pieces in two or three colours, wear your bulkiest shoes and layers while travelling and plan one wash. Cold trips are harder because coats and jumpers take space, so wear the heaviest outfit while travelling and cut back on shoes and bottoms.

faq.q: How do you pack a capsule wardrobe for cold weather?
faq.a: Build it around layers rather than many separate outfits: two thin base layers, a couple of long-sleeved tops, a jumper, a packable mid-layer and one warm coat. Wear the coat, boots and heaviest jumper while travelling. Keep to two pairs of shoes and three bottoms, and add a hat, gloves and scarf as your accessory set.
